source.suraNameGloss: The Inevitable / The Event (sura name; not translated as content)
source.primary_manuscript: Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (BnF Arabe 328 + St. Petersburg, National Library of Russia, Marcel 18 / 13 et al. + Birmingham, Cadbury Research Library Mingana 1572a + Vatican, BAV Vat. ar. 1605/1 fragments)
source.primary_manuscript_dating: Hijazi script; late 7th century CE — radiocarbon analyses of dispersed fragments yielded ranges placing this manuscript-group among the earliest-known Qur'anic witnesses (Birmingham/Oxford 2015 radiocarbon report on Mingana 1572a: 95.4% probability 568–645 CE); the broader codex is conventionally dated to the late 7th century on palaeographic grounds (Déroche 2009).
source.primary_manuscript_contains: Approximately 45% of the Qur'an across the dispersed fragments; includes Suras 53–56 in a continuous run in BnF Arabe 328a — Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah is preserved in this run; the ayahs 15–24 fall within the preserved-folio scope.
source.cross_collation_manuscript: Sanʿāʾ 1 palimpsest (the lower text C-1; Yemen, Dar al-Makhtutat) — consulted for orthographic-norm comparison; the Sanʿāʾ 1 lower text DOES preserve portions of Sura 56 per Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 §4 catalogue, with documented orthographic and (limited) lexical variants — though for the specific ayah-range 15–24 the Sanʿāʾ 1 evidence is partial. Tübingen Ma VI 165 does not preserve Sura 56 (its scope is Suras 17–36).
source.reference_vocalization: Cairo 1924 King Fuad edition (Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim reading-tradition) — the standard printed Qur'an.
source.transliteration_convention: DMG (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft) scientific transliteration: ʾ for hamza, ʿ for ʿayn, ḥ for ḥāʾ, ṭ ḍ ṣ ẓ for emphatic consonants, ġ for ghayn, ḫ for khāʾ, ṯ for thāʾ, ḏ for dhāl, š for shīn, macrons for long vowels.
source.verificationStatus: best-effort reconstruction; verification pending against the BnF original codicology (Arabe 328a), the Déroche 2009 facsimile-edition apparatus, the Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 Sanʿāʾ 1 lower-text transcription for the Sura 56 ayah-range, and the Corpus Coranicum digital comparative apparatus. The rasm for Sura 56:15-24 is well-attested and stable across the early Hijazi witnesses; the Cairo Hafs reading supplied as the reference vocalization.
source.fetchedFrom: Corpus Coranicum digital apparatus (corpuscoranicum.de) for the rasm-skeleton and variant apparatus; Tanzil.net Cairo Hafs text for the reference vocalization; Déroche 2009 + Sadeghi-Bergmann 2010 + Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 for codicological framing.
source.citation: Déroche, François, La transmission écrite du Coran dans les débuts de l'islam: le codex Parisino-petropolitanus (Brill 2009); Déroche, François, Qur'ans of the Umayyads (Brill 2014); Sadeghi, Behnam, and Bergmann, Uwe, 'The Codex of a Companion of the Prophet and the Qurʾān of the Prophet' (Arabica 57, 2010); Sadeghi, Behnam, and Goudarzi, Mohsen, 'Sanʿāʾ 1 and the Origins of the Qurʾān' (Der Islam 87, 2010); Hilali, Asma, The Sanaa Palimpsest (Oxford 2017); Neuwirth, Angelika, Scripture, Poetry, and the Making of a Community (Oxford 2014); Reynolds, Gabriel Said (ed.), The Qur'ān in Its Historical Context (Routledge 2008/2011); Andrew Rippin, 'The Qur'ān and its Interpretive Tradition' (Variorum 2001); Maher Jarrar, 'Houris', Encyclopaedia of the Qur'ān (Brill 2002); Tor Andrae, Der Ursprung des Islams und das Christentum (Uppsala 1926); Christoph Luxenberg, Die syro-aramäische Lesart des Koran (Berlin 2000) — the controversial 'white grapes' re-reading of *ḥūr* discussed and largely rejected in mainstream scholarship (e.g., Devin Stewart's response, 2007/2008); Corpus Coranicum project (BBAW, Berlin); Tanzil.net.
source.paleography_note: The `rasm` field provides the consonantal skeleton without vowel marks (tashkīl). Letter-discrimination dots (iʿjām) are absent in the original Hijazi manuscripts for the letter-families that share an identical skeletal shape. The `rasm_paleography_note` field on each ayah documents which specific letters in that ayah would appear without their dots in the manuscript. Hamza was not marked in the earliest Hijazi manuscripts; tāʾ-marbūṭa was written as undifferentiated hāʾ.
source.rasmConventionNote: Rasm rendered as: tashkīl-stripped, hamza-glyphs collapsed to underlying carrier, tāʾ-marbūṭa rendered as hāʾ. Letter-shapes preserved as modern codepoints, with the `rasm_paleography_note` documenting which letters are affected by the absence of iʿjām dots.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters in Codex Parisino-petropolitanus: *ʿayn* of على (already dotless in dotted manuscripts; here the lower-bowl initial-form); *sīn* of سرر (toothed three-tooth skeleton without the upper three dots that distinguish shīn from sīn — in the rasm سرر could in principle be read as a sequence with shīn, but the lexical context resolves this); *nūn* of موضونه (medial single-tooth indistinguishable from b/t/th/y); *ḍād* of موضونه (dotless ṣ/ḍ skeleton — ḍād is distinguished from ṣād only by an upper dot in dotted manuscripts). **TĀʾ-MARBŪṬA**: موضونه is written with a final hāʾ-shape ه in the early manuscripts; modern Cairo orthography has موضونة with the tāʾ-marbūṭa ة dots — a later scribal-reform addition. The double-rāʾ of سرر is a defective-scripting case typical of short-vowel patterns in Hijazi orthography.
ayahs.notes: **MAJOR THEME — opening of the paradisal-reception description for the *as-sābiqūna s-sābiqūn* 'the foremost ones'.** This ayah opens the paradise-furnishings description for the foremost-of-the-foremost (introduced in v. 10-14). The *surur* 'couches/thrones' (sing. *sarīr*) is a recurrent paradisal-furnishings term (cf. 15:47, 37:44, 43:34, 52:20, 56:15, 88:13); *mawḍūnah* is variously glossed as 'woven', 'inlaid with gold/jewels', 'closely-wrought' (al-Ṭabarī cites multiple early authorities — Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid — with slight semantic shadings). **RAËLIAN CANON LENS-RISK SITE**: this 10-ayah passage is engaged in *Extra-Terrestrials Took Me To Their Planet* (Raël 1977) and is read by the canon as a description of the paradisal-planet reception (cloning-immortality + companion-civilization on the Elohim home planet); the canon's reading layers a sci-fi-paradisal-reception onto the Quranic description. Operational disavowal required in the apparatus. Cross-corpus: cf. Esth 1:6 (the Persian-king reception-couches as a literary type); cf. the Sumerian/Akkadian banqueting-scene iconography (Anzu, Ishtar reliefs); cf. Rev 7:9-17 (the white-robed throng before the throne). **NEUWIRTH 2014**: reads this passage as the eschatological-banquet topos, the Quranic distinct realization of a Near-Eastern eschatological-feast tradition documented from Isa 25:6-8 onward (the cosmic feast on Mount Zion).

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *tāʾ* of متكين and of متقبلين (medial single-tooth — indistinguishable from b/th/n/y); *kāf* of متكين (the initial/medial kāf has a distinctive double-stroke shape that distinguishes it from the b/t/th/n/y group); *yāʾ* of متكين and of متقبلين (medial single-tooth); *nūn* of متكين and of متقبلين (final hook-form); *qāf* of متقبلين (dotless ڡ-skeleton); *bāʾ* of متقبلين (medial single-tooth). **PALEOGRAPHIC NOTE**: متكين is written in the early manuscripts and in the Uthmanic orthography with a single-tooth kāf-sequence representing the Form VIII participle *muttakiʾīn* 'reclining'; modern Cairo orthography retains this defective scripting (مُتَّكِـِٔينَ with the hamza-on-yāʾ ـِٔ as a later orthographic addition).
ayahs.notes: THEME — the reclining-and-facing-one-another posture of the paradisal reception. *muttakiʾīn* 'reclining' is the standard Greco-Roman-Eastern symposium / banquet-couch posture (cf. the *triclinium*; cf. Jewish *Pesaḥ haggadah* reclining-as-free-person trope); *mutaqābilīn* 'facing one another' is the symposium's communal-conviviality gesture. The pairing is a recurrent Quranic paradise-description (cf. 15:47, 18:31, 37:44, 37:53, 52:20, 56:16). Cross-corpus: cf. Luke 14:15-24 / Matt 22:1-14 (the messianic-banquet parable); cf. m. Pesaḥim 10:1 (the Passover-reclining halakhah); cf. Isa 25:6 (the Yahweh-banquet on Mount Zion). **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: part of the 10-ayah passage engaged by the canon; the reclining-and-facing pose is layered with the canon's paradisal-companion-civilization framing.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *yāʾ* of يطوف (initial single-tooth); *ṭāʾ* of يطوف (dotless ṭ/ẓ skeleton — ṭāʾ has no upper dot in dotted manuscripts, ẓāʾ has one; in rasm they are indistinguishable but lexical disambiguation is immediate); *fāʾ* of يطوف (dotless ڡ-skeleton at end of word — fāʾ has a single upper dot in dotted manuscripts, qāf has two; in rasm both are dotless and indistinguishable); *yāʾ* of عليهم (medial single-tooth); *nūn* of ولدن and of مخلدون (final hook-form indistinguishable from b/t/th/y/n in medial position, but final-form curve makes nūn recognisable in final position); *dāl* of ولدن and of مخلدون (dāl/dhāl indistinguishable — dāl is dotless, dhāl has an upper dot in dotted manuscripts); *khāʾ* of مخلدون (dotless j/ḥ/kh skeleton). **NOTABLE**: ولدن is written defectively in the Uthmanic orthography without the medial alif of plural — modern reading is *wildān* (or *wuldān*) 'youths/boys/lads', plural of *walad*. This is a defective-scripting case typical of Hijazi orthography.
ayahs.notes: **MAJOR THEME and MAJOR LENS-RISK SITE — the *wildān muḫalladūn* 'immortalized youths'.** Modern translations render variously: 'eternal youths', 'youths of perpetual freshness', 'immortal boys', 'youths who do not age'. The participle *muḫalladūn* (Form II passive of ḫ-l-d 'to be eternal/lasting') is variously parsed as 'eternally-youthful' (their youth never fades) or 'immortalized' (they never die) — classical tafsīr (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī) preserves both readings without firm preference. The serving-youths topos is a Greco-Roman-Eastern banquet-iconography element (cf. the Sasanian banqueting-scene reliefs; cf. the Greek *kylix*-symposium serving-boys). Cross-corpus: cf. the Zoroastrian afterlife *Hadhokht Nask* / *Mēnōg ī Khrad* paradise-attendants tradition; cf. Rev 7:15 (the servants before the throne); cf. 1 En. 32:6 (the immortal-tree paradise-attendants). **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: this is the highest-density ayah within the Sura 56 passage for the canon's cloning-immortality / paradisal-companion-civilization layering — the *muḫallad* 'eternalized' descriptor is read by the canon as a description of cloning-derived immortality on the Elohim home planet. **CONTROVERSY**: Christoph Luxenberg 2000 (Die syro-aramäische Lesart des Koran) controversially proposed re-reading *wildān muḫalladūn* via Syriac-Aramaic substrate as 'fruits everlasting'; this re-reading has been largely rejected by mainstream Quranic scholarship (cf. Devin Stewart's response 2007/2008; Angelika Neuwirth's response in Reynolds ed. 2008). Operational disavowal required for both the Raëlian-canon layering and the Luxenberg re-reading — preserve the mainstream Arabic-philological reading (immortalized youths) and document the disputes.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *bāʾ* of باكواب and of واباريق (initial single-tooth) and of باكواب-final (final single-tooth) and of واباريق-medial (medial single-tooth); *kāf* of باكواب and of واباريق and of وكاس (initial/medial kāf double-stroke); *yāʾ* of واباريق (medial single-tooth); *qāf* of واباريق (dotless ڡ-skeleton at end of word); *sīn* of وكاس (toothed three-tooth skeleton); *nūn* of من and of معين (final hook); *ʿayn* of معين (already dotless); *yāʾ* of معين (medial single-tooth). **PALEOGRAPHIC NOTE**: the orthographic-cluster باكواب واباريق represents the goblets-and-ewers-and-cups paradisal-vessels topos; the rasm is dense with similar-looking single-tooth and dotless-bowl skeletons that the recitation-tradition disambiguates by memorized phonology.
ayahs.notes: THEME — the paradisal-drinking-vessels. *akwāb* (sing. *kūb*) = 'goblets/cups' (loanword from Greek *kúpē* / Aramaic *kūbā*); *abārīq* (sing. *ibrīq*) = 'ewers/pitchers' (Persian loanword *ābrīz*); *kaʾs* = 'cup/chalice' (cognate with Hebrew *kōs*); *maʿīn* = 'flowing water/spring/source'. The drinking-cup-trinity is a paradisal-feast iconographic set. Cross-corpus: cf. Ps 23:5 ('thou preparest a table before me ... my cup runneth over'); cf. Isa 25:6 ('a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow'); cf. Rev 22:1 ('a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal'); cf. the Sasanian iconography of the king holding the *kūbā* / *kāsa*. **NEUWIRTH 2014**: reads the loanword-density of this ayah as evidence of the Qurʾān's situatedness in the multi-lingual late-antique Near East. **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: part of the 10-ayah passage; the canon's reading layers a sci-fi paradisal-reception onto these vessel-iconographic terms.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *yāʾ* of يصدعون and of ينزفون (initial single-tooth); *ṣād* of يصدعون (dotless ṣ/ḍ skeleton); *dāl* of يصدعون (dāl/dhāl indistinguishable in rasm); *ʿayn* of يصدعون and of عنها (already dotless); *nūn* of يصدعون and of عنها and of ينزفون (final or medial hook); *zāy* of ينزفون (dotless r/z skeleton — rāʾ has no dot, zāy has one upper dot in dotted manuscripts); *fāʾ* of ينزفون (dotless ڡ-skeleton). The ayah's rasm is highly resistant to mis-reading despite the dotless-letter density because the verbs *yuṣaddaʿūna* 'they are afflicted with headache' and *yunzafūna* 'they are intoxicated/depleted' are lexically distinctive.
ayahs.notes: THEME — the paradisal-wine-without-effects clause. 'They get no headache from it, nor do they become intoxicated/depleted.' This is the standard Quranic paradisal-wine differentiator from earthly wine, which the Qurʾān condemns (cf. 2:219, 5:90-91): paradisal *khamr* is wine-without-the-pathologies. *yuṣaddaʿūn* 'they are afflicted with headache' (from *ṣudāʿ* 'headache'); *yunzafūn* 'they are emptied/intoxicated' (the verb-form is debated: classical tafsīr divides between 'they do not run out [of wine]' and 'they do not become drunk' — al-Ṭabarī preserves both readings). Cf. 37:46-47 (the parallel formulation: لَا فِيهَا غَوْلٌ وَلَا هُمْ عَنْهَا يُنزَفُونَ 'no ill-effect in it, nor are they depleted'). Cross-corpus: cf. Isa 25:6 ('wines on the lees well refined'); cf. the rabbinic tradition of paradisal *yayin ha-meshummar* 'preserved wine' (b. Berakhot 34b, b. Sanhedrin 99a). **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: part of the 10-ayah passage; the canon's reading layers the no-side-effects-paradisal-substance frame onto the canon's planet-of-the-Elohim eternal-pleasures framing.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *fāʾ* of وفكهه (dotless ڡ-skeleton initial); *kāf* of وفكهه (medial kāf); *yāʾ* of يتخيرون (initial single-tooth); *tāʾ* of يتخيرون (medial single-tooth); *khāʾ* of يتخيرون (dotless j/ḥ/kh skeleton — khāʾ has an upper dot in dotted manuscripts, ḥāʾ is dotless, jīm has a lower dot; in rasm all three indistinguishable); *nūn* of يتخيرون (final hook). **TĀʾ-MARBŪṬA**: وفكهه is written with a final hāʾ-shape ه in the early manuscripts; modern Cairo orthography has وَفَاكِهَةٍ with tāʾ-marbūṭa ة. The defective-vs-plene scripting of فاكهه/فكهه is variable across early manuscripts: the Hijazi orthographic preference is the defective form (no medial alif).
ayahs.notes: THEME — the paradisal-fruit. *fākiha* (sing.) is the collective 'fruit' (cognate with Aramaic *piqqehā*); *yataḫayyarūn* 'they choose for themselves / they select' (Form V of ḫ-y-r 'good/choice'). The fruit-of-choice paradisal-element is recurrent (cf. 36:57, 37:42, 38:51, 43:73, 44:55, 52:22, 55:52, 56:20, 56:32, 77:42). Cross-corpus: cf. Gen 2:9 (the Garden of Eden's *kol-ʿēṣ neḥmād lĕ-marʾeh wĕ-ṭōv lĕ-maʾăkāl* 'every tree pleasant to sight and good for food'); cf. Rev 22:2 (the tree of life bearing twelve manner of fruits); cf. the Zoroastrian paradisal-fruit tradition. **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: part of the 10-ayah passage.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *ḥāʾ* of ولحم (dotless j/ḥ/kh skeleton); *ṭāʾ* of طير (dotless ṭ/ẓ skeleton — ṭāʾ is dotless, ẓāʾ has an upper dot in dotted manuscripts); *yāʾ* of طير and of يشتهون (medial/initial single-tooth); *shīn* of يشتهون (toothed three-tooth skeleton without the upper three dots that distinguish shīn from sīn); *tāʾ* of يشتهون (medial single-tooth); *nūn* of يشتهون (final hook). The *ḥm* of ولحم and *yr* of طير are both dotless-letter sequences that the lexical context (lahm-flesh, ṭayr-bird) disambiguates.
ayahs.notes: THEME — the paradisal-bird-meat. *laḥm ṭayr* 'flesh of fowl' is a hapax legomenon in the Qurʾān (only here); *yaštahūn* 'they desire' (Form VIII of š-h-w/y 'to desire'). Cross-corpus: cf. Num 11:31-34 (the quail provided in the wilderness, though as a chastisement); cf. the Mesopotamian paradisal-feast bird-iconography. The roast-bird as a paradisal-banquet element is documented in classical tafsīr with various ḥadīth specifying particular birds (al-Ṭabarī cites multiple early authorities). **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: part of the 10-ayah passage.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *ḥāʾ* of وحور (dotless j/ḥ/kh skeleton); *yāʾ* of عين (medial single-tooth); *ʿayn* of عين (already dotless). The rasm is a 5-letter sequence (و-ح-و-ر + ع-ي-ن) representing two words; the lexical content is famous and stable.
ayahs.notes: **MAJOR THEME, MAJOR LENS-RISK SITE — the *ḥūr ʿīn* 'wide-eyed companions' (the famous 'houris of paradise').** The phrase *ḥūr ʿīn* (lit. 'white(-eyed) ones, wide(-eyed)') is the most-discussed and most-misunderstood paradisal-element in the Qurʾān in non-Muslim reception. *ḥūr* is the plural of *ḥawrāʾ* (feminine) / *aḥwar* (masculine), meaning 'one whose eye-white is intensely white and whose iris is intensely dark', a beauty-descriptor in pre-Islamic Arabian poetry (the *muʿallaqāt* corpus); *ʿīn* is the plural of *aʿyan* / *ʿaynāʾ* 'wide-eyed' (large pupils). The phrase occurs at 44:54, 52:20, 56:22 (here). The Qurʾān itself does NOT specify gender of the ḥūr in this ayah or elsewhere; the assumption of 'female paradisal companions' is a tafsīr-tradition development (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) reading these as the *companion-houris* alongside the human female partners of the believers. **ORIENTALIST STEREOTYPE FLAG**: the 'houris of paradise' as 'celestial virgins' is a heavily-orientalist-distorted Western-pop interpretation that mainstream Islamic theology and modern Arabic-philological scholarship reject in its sensationalist form (no '72 virgins' enumeration appears in the Qurʾān; the figure is from a weak *ḥadīth* tradition contested in *ḥadīth*-criticism literature). **LUXENBERG CONTROVERSY**: Christoph Luxenberg 2000 controversially proposed re-reading *ḥūr ʿīn* via Syriac-Aramaic substrate as 'white grapes' / 'white raisins' — this re-reading has been largely rejected by mainstream scholarship (Devin Stewart 2007/2008; Angelika Neuwirth in Reynolds ed. 2008). **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: this ayah is the headline-ayah of the 10-ayah passage as engaged by the canon; the canon's reading layers a paradisal-companion-civilization (specifically: female biological-clones / advanced-civilization-companion) frame onto the *ḥūr ʿīn* description. Operational disavowal required: distinguish the canon's reading from (a) the orientalist 'virgins' stereotype, (b) the Luxenberg re-reading, (c) the mainstream Islamic theological reading. Maher Jarrar's 'Houris' article in the Encyclopaedia of the Qur'ān (Brill 2002) is the standard reference. Cross-corpus: cf. Rev 14:4 (the 144,000 'virgins'); cf. the Zoroastrian *daēnā* paradisal-companion-figure (the spiritualized soul-companion of the deceased); cf. the rabbinic *tzeniʿōt* paradisal-companions tradition (less developed).

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *kāf* of كامثل (initial kāf); *thāʾ* of كامثل (in dotted manuscripts three upper dots; in rasm a single-tooth indistinguishable from b/t/n/y); *nūn* of المكنون (×2, medial and final). **NOTABLE**: اللولو is the Uthmanic-orthographic spelling of *al-luʾluʾ* 'the pearl' — the early manuscripts write this without the hamza-glyphs (which are a later orthographic addition); the modern Cairo edition preserves اللُّؤْلُؤِ with hamza-glyphs. The defective-scripting اللولو is the underlying Hijazi rasm. The *المكنون* is the standard 'hidden/concealed/well-kept' descriptor, with stable rasm.
ayahs.notes: THEME — the simile of the well-kept pearl. The *ḥūr ʿīn* are compared to *al-luʾluʾ al-maknūn* 'the hidden/preserved pearl' — a beauty-and-preservation simile. *Maknūn* 'kept hidden, treasured-up' (passive participle of k-n-n 'to conceal/treasure'); the parallel formulation 'pearls hidden in shells' appears at 52:24 and 76:19 (in the *wildān muḫalladūn* context as well). Cross-corpus: cf. Matt 13:45-46 (the parable of the pearl of great price); cf. Cant 4:9-10 (the praise of the bride's beauty as a treasured gem); cf. the Sasanian iconography of the king's *durr* / royal pearl. The pearl-as-preserved-beauty topos is documented across the late-antique Near Eastern literary corpus. **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: part of the 10-ayah passage; the simile-rhetoric coheres with the canon's reading of the paradisal-companion as a preserved/curated being.

ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *jīm* of جزاء (dotless j/ḥ/kh skeleton — jīm has a lower dot in dotted manuscripts, ḥāʾ is dotless, khāʾ has an upper dot; in rasm all three indistinguishable); *zāy* of جزاء (dotless r/z skeleton — rāʾ has no dot, zāy has one upper dot in dotted manuscripts); *bāʾ* of بما (initial single-tooth); *nūn* of كانوا and of يعملون (final/medial hook); *yāʾ* of يعملون (initial single-tooth); *ʿayn* of يعملون (already dotless). **PALEOGRAPHIC NOTE**: the word جزاء in the earliest Hijazi orthography is typically written جزا (without final hamza-bearing alif-mamdūda) — the hamza-glyph was not yet developed. The modern Cairo orthography supplies the hamza جَزَآءًۢ as a later orthographic addition. The Hijazi rasm reads جزا for this word.
ayahs.notes: **CLOSING THEME — the recompense formula.** 'A reward for what they used to do.' This is the standard Quranic recompense-statement closing the paradisal-reception description, situating the entire paradisal-banquet as the *jazāʾ* 'reward/recompense' for righteous deeds. The recompense-by-deeds formula is recurrent (cf. 35:32-35, 37:39-43, 52:19, 56:24, 77:43). Cross-corpus: cf. Matt 16:27 ('then he shall reward every man according to his works'); cf. Rev 22:12 ('my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be'); cf. m. Avot 2:16 ('it is not your responsibility to finish the work, but neither are you free to desist from it; if you have studied much Torah, your reward shall be increased'). The Quranic recompense-formula sits within the Jewish-Christian-Quranic *erga / maʿasim / aʿmāl* 'works' tradition. **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: closing ayah of the 10-ayah passage; the recompense-frame closes the paradisal-reception sequence and ties it to ethical-deeds, which the canon's reading retains (the Elohim-paradisal-companionship as reward for civilizational contribution). **PALEOGRAPHIC**: this is the final ayah of the WoH-selected passage; in Codex Parisino-petropolitanus the sura continues for many more ayahs on subsequent folios (the sura is 96 ayahs long).
